knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 71-year-old male from Madrid, Spain, presented with a 2-month history of dysphonia. He has a 30-year history of smoking and underwent a liver transplant 8 years ago due to liver cirrhosis, currently on chronic immunosuppressant therapy with mycophenolate mofetil. The patient exhibited symptoms including dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, autophony, fatigue, anorexia, and a weight loss of over 20 kg in the past 6 months. Fiber-optic laryngoscopy identified a vegetative lesion on the lingual surface of the epiglottis, extending to the epiglottic vallecula. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan showed increased soft tissue size on the lingual surface of the epiglottis.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Histoplasmosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Histoplasmosis.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Subacute Histoplasmosis

knowledge_fragments.content: Although using time duration to categorize cough seems easy and attractive, the presumed precision of duration to define a cough as acute, subacute, or chronic (and the differential diagnostic implied) is less precise and the issue more complex then it appears. Obviously, all cough at its beginning is acute. It is not currently possible to predict at the onset of cough in whom it will be of short duration (i.e., resolve within 3 weeks) or in whom it will become subacute or chronic. The issue is further complicated by the fact that effective therapy can abort or abbreviate the duration of cough, whereas failure to institute effective therapy can convert what might have been an acute cough into a subacute or chronic one. Furthermore, recurrent acute episodes of cough can be a manifestation of an undiagnosed chronic disease (e.g., asthma). Nevertheless, keeping these caveats in mind, a relatively “standard” diagnostic and therapeutic approach based on duration of cough has proved useful.
knowledge_fragments.title: Clinical approach to acute cough. > Problems with Definition

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: An 8-year-old girl arrived at the emergency room with a history of abdominal pain lasting one week, accompanied by fever for two days, diarrhea, and vomiting. Her parents had tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 six weeks earlier, although she had not shown any symptoms at that time. Upon examination, she was found to have an elevated heart rate but maintained normal blood pressure and body temperature. Physical examination revealed widespread abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the right lower quadrant, along with mild guarding. No noticeable changes were observed in her skin or mucous membranes.. Confirmed diagnosis: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children. Differential diagnosis includes: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 40-year-old man with skin phototype IV presented with a 1-month history of multiple reddish skin lesions located on the anterior chest, neck, and upper back. The patient reported photosensitivity and intermittent joint pain. He denied any history of prior drug intake. Physical examination of the skin revealed multiple erythematous, scaly papules and annular plaques, with some plaques exhibiting a peripheral rim of white scales.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 36-year-old male presented with shortness of breath and swelling in the lower extremities for the past 2 weeks. The patient also reported experiencing intermittent fever over the last 2 months. Upon admission, vital signs included a heart rate of 103 beats per minute, blood pressure of 122/47 mmHg, and a temperature of 37.2°C. Cardiac examination identified a pandiastolic murmur in the aortic region. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated NT-proBNP level of 4492.0 pg/mL.. Confirmed diagnosis: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Subacute Bacterial Endocarditis.

knowledge_fragments.content:
Evaluation 
 Pregnancy test in all females of childbearing age — this is mandatory
 Vitals: Tachycardia and hypotension suggest serious pathology (hemorrhage, sepsis, perforation)
 Point-of-care ultrasound: FAST exam (free fluid), RUQ (gallbladder), aorta (AAA), renal (hydronephrosis)
 Workup is by location:
 RUQ pain
 RLQ pain
 Epigastric pain
 LUQ pain
 LLQ pain
 Diffuse abdominal pain
 Flank pain
knowledge_fragments.title: Abdominal pain > Evaluation

knowledge_fragments.content:
Diagnosis may be obvious in a child who has unexplained severe pleuritic or abdominal pain during an

epidemic. However, in other situations, symptoms may be hard to distinguish from those due to other

conditions that cause chest or abdominal pain.

Laboratory diagnosis is not routinely necessary; it consists of isolating the virus in a throat or stool culture

or, less commonly, demonstrating seroconversion.

B5.label: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome

tree.case_summary:
A 45-year-old African American woman presents to her primary care physician for not feeling well. She states she has had a cough for the past week. She also has abdominal pain and trouble focusing that has been worsening and has lost 5 pounds recently. Her gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) has been poorly controlled recently. The patient is a non-smoker and has a history of GERD for which she takes antacids. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 115/71 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min. A physical exam is within normal limits. Laboratory studies are ordered and are below:

Serum:
Na+: 139 mEq/L
K+: 4.1 mEq/L
Cl-: 101 mEq/L
HCO3-: 24 mEq/L
Urea nitrogen: 12 mg/dL
Glucose: 70 mg/dL
Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL
Ca2+: 12.5 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase: 150 U/L
Phosphorus: 2.0 mg/dL

Urine:
Color: amber
Nitrites: negative
Sodium: 5 mmol/24 hours
Red blood cells: 0/hpf

Which of the following is the most likely explanation of this patient's current presentation?

Options:
A. Antacid overuse
B. Increased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
C. Increased parathyroid hormone
D. Malignancy
E. Viral illness

excluded_candidates: Gastrointestinal infection: less likely due to absence of fever and normal physical exam
Pulmonary embolism: less likely due to absence of chest pain and shortness of breath
root.label: Subacute Multisystem Syndrome with Abdominal Pain, Cough, and Constitutional Alarm Signs
